articles.title: 'Already suffered losses': Traders' body urges Rahul Gandhi to defer Delhi rally
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Chamber of Trade and Industry on Saturday urged Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi to postpone the INDIA bloc's upcoming rally on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Chamber of Trade and Industry on Saturday urged Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi to postpone the INDIA bloc's upcoming rally on November 1 at Ramlila Maidan, saying the demonstration could disrupt business worth Rs 10,000 crore during the peak Diwali shopping season.In a letter to Rahul, CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal said the rally could affect wholesale and retail markets around Ramlila Maidan at a time when traders expect heavy customer footfall ahead of Dhanteras and Diwali."This year, Dhanteras falls on Friday, November 6, Diwali on November 8 and Bhai Dooj on November 10. People begin shopping for Dhanteras and Diwali a week in advance. In Delhi alone, Dhanteras-related business across sectors such as gold and silver, utensils, electronics, textiles, dry fruits, sweets, automobiles, vehicles, property and gift items amounts to approximately Rs 25,000 crore. This trade is the backbone of Delhi's economy," the letter reads.The traders' body said markets generally see increased activity about a week before the festivals, making the timing of the rally a matter of concern.Goyal also said traders in Delhi had already suffered losses of around Rs 3,000 crore in October due to rallies, marches and road closures in Connaught Place, India Gate and central Delhi."According to CTI's estimates, traders in Delhi have already suffered losses of approximately Rs 3,000 crore due to repeated rallies, marches and road closures in Connaught Place, India Gate and central Delhi," he said."The movement of goods into wholesale markets had come to a halt, while retail customers were unable to reach the markets," he added.The organisation also pointed to around 20 wholesale and retail markets within a five-kilometre radius of Ramlila Maidan, including Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazar, Chawri Bazar, Bhagirath Palace, Khari Baoli, Kashmere Gate, Nai Sarak, Mori Gate, Kinari Bazar, Dariba, Daryaganj, Ajmeri Gate, Jama Masjid, Karol Bagh and Azad Market."Goods from these markets are supplied across the country. Traffic diversions, metro station closures and barricading during the rally could bring business in these markets to a complete standstill," Goyal said.While acknowledging the right to peaceful protest and democratic expression, CTI urged political parties to avoid holding large rallies in key commercial areas until the festival period ends.The opposition rally aims to ramp up pressure on the government over the "vote chori" issue and demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.On October 12, protests over the "vote theft" charge reached the Supreme Court's doorstep, with opposition leaders, activists and civil society members participating in a 'March for Democracy' along a heavily barricaded route in Delhi and filing a joint petition against the SIR.Rahul hosted INDIA bloc leaders for tea at his home on October 13. After the meeting, the opposition bloc vowed to continue resisting and take the "vote chori" fight to its logical conclusion.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2014, researchers spread cocoa pod husks around near-dead cacao trees in Nigeria; two years later, pod production reportedly rose 64% and 68% at two sites
articles.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that cocoa pod husks can significantly rejuvenate dying cacao trees, boosting pod production by 64% and 68% at two Nigerian sites.
articles.body: Cocoa farms in south-western Nigeria produce large volumes of pod husks, the outer shells left once the beans are removed. Although most of these farms treat these husks as waste, it is important to know that these wastes are nutrient-rich and can be added as an effective soil additive to aging plantations. Indeed, the researchers at the Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria have carried out experiments on their use. In one of their experiments, the researchers wanted to explore the effects of adding husks to dying trees. They asked if these husks would rejuvenate the dying trees to start producing again. The figures from this experiment have now been simplified into a percentage increase in the number of pods. As the paper shows, the figures are more complicated and the experiment involved more than husks alone.The May 2014 to December 2017 husk trial at Ibadan and OwenaThe trial is described in Rehabilitation of Old and Moribund Cacao Soil Using Organic Amendments in Ibadan and Owena of South West Nigeria, published on 25 March 2020 in the Journal of Scientific Research and Reports. This experiment occurred between May 2014 and December 2017 on two farms, situated in Ibadan in Oyo State and Owena in Ondo State. Uninfested fresh pods were first oven-dried before grinding them to 4 mm sieve size. These were then spread around the trees during the rainy-season months of April/May and August/September. According to the paper, the experiment used a randomized complete block design with four treatments and four replications, with amendments applied to eight cacao trees per plot.After two years, the abstract of the paper reports higher pod production: at Ibadan, cocoa pod husk alone gave the largest increase, 64% above the control, while at Owena the three amended treatments raised yields by 68%, 64% and 63%, respectively. These figures come from a trial that also tested husk blended with neem leaf powder, so they need careful interpretation. Husk was used individually in an amount of 0.5 kg per tree. Two other treatments mixed husk with neem leaf powder in ratios of 90:10 and 80:20, respectively. Unprotected trees were used as controls. The whole paper is available on the website of the Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria.Pod counts of 64 and 68 per tree and why the percentage claim needs careIt can be observed from the abstract that even after two years, only husk has recorded the maximum percentage pod gain against the control at 64% at Ibadan and at Owena, husk has a value of 68%, whereas the neem blends are 64 and 63%. In the results section, it looks like the comparison is of pods only. According to the results section of the paper in the Journal of Scientific Research and Reports, pod counts on husk-treated trees rose from 40 to 64 at Ibadan and from 47 to 68 at Owena. That is an increase of about 60% and 45%, respectively, which does not match the 64% and 68% reported in the abstract. The abstract appears to compare treated trees with the control, while these counts compare pod numbers before and after treatment.The results section appears to compare 2012 and 2013, even though the trial ran from May 2014 to December 2017. In the study, changes in soil composition have been reported by the authors. The pH of soil has increased from 6.50 to 6.89 at Ibadan and from 6.41 to 6.82 at Owena, while more nitrogen has been released eight months after application. Authors have credited part of the increase in pods to weeding and pruning.The Ondo and Osun compost trial and its 72.4% bean yield gainIntegrated Soil Fertility Management for Smallholder Cocoa Farms: Using Combination of Cocoa Pod Husk Based Compost and Mineral Fertilizers, published on 21 March 2020 in the International Journal of Plant and Soil Science, takes a different route. The husks were cut and composted together with chicken droppings and Chromolaena odorata leaf mulch in a ratio of 2:1 and applied at 4 kg/tree in four villages in Ondo and Osun States. The experiment was laid out using five treatments with three replications, 10 trees/treatment/block. The abstract shows increases in dry bean yields of 72.4% and 36.4% over the control for compost mixed with NPK fertilizer and compost or NPK fertilizer alone respectively. From the same study, Table 7 shows site-wise increases of 60.0 to 75.0% for the compost and NPK mixture and 30.0 to 41.7% for compost alone, so the 72.4% reported in the abstract does not match any single site figure in the table.Black pod risk, unused husks and the nutrients lost with each harvestThe same paper adds that husks left on the farm could host and transmit Phytophthora inoculum that causes black pod. The paper says that all of the farmers interviewed did not use their farm-produced husks (100%) and no farmer had used any fertilizer before the experiment. Compost with NPK reduced black pod damage, with percentage loss levels of 9.9 to 13.4% compared to 32.2 to 35.5% in the control. The paper further refers to previous research, which shows that harvesting 1000 kilograms of dry beans leads to the loss of 20 kilograms of nitrogen, 4 kilograms of phosphorus and 10 kilograms of potassium from the soil, explaining the importance of nutrient replacement.The above-mentioned trial of husks relieved the disease concern through the use of fresh and uncontaminated pods, which were dried and milled prior to application, even though the trial did not evaluate black pod disease. Both studies indicate that husks may be beneficial to exhausted plantations, depending on how they are handled and farm surroundings. Neither study provides a straightforward, conclusive measure of the effect of husks alone: the first trial’s figures raise unresolved questions and the second tested composted husk mixed with other materials.You use AI every day. articles.title: Delhi court orders trial of Yasin Malik, Engineer Rashid among 7 in Rs 8.94 crore money laundering case linked to hawala funding from Pakistan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A court in New Delhi has ordered a trial against jailed separatist leader Yasin Malik, Baramulla MP Sheikh Abdul Rashid, alias Engineer Rashid,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A court in New Delhi has ordered a trial against jailed separatist leader Yasin Malik, Baramulla MP Sheikh Abdul Rashid, alias Engineer Rashid, and five others in a Rs 8.94 crore money laundering case linked to alleged funding from Pakistan through hawala channels for secessionist activities in Jammu and Kashmir.Special Judge Prashant Sharma ordered the framing of charges against the seven accused under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), observing that the material on record raised strong suspicion of their involvement in the offence.The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has alleged that proceeds of crime worth Rs 8.94 crore were generated and received by the accused and subsequently routed, transferred, concealed, possessed, acquired and used through various channels.Yasin Malik, Engineer Rashid among 7 accusedThe accused include Malik, chief of the banned Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF); separatist leader Shabir Ahmad Shah; Baramulla MP Sheikh Abdul Rashid, alias Engineer Rashid; Masarat Alam; Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali; Naval Kishore Kapoor; and M/s Trison Farms and Constructions Pvt Ltd.The ED's case stems from a 2017 case registered by the National Investigation Agency (NIA), in which charges were invoked under various provisions of the Indian Penal Code and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).ED alleges Pakistan funding The prosecution has alleged that the accused received funds from the "Pakistani establishment" through hawala channels and other means to promote secessionist activities and carry out acts prejudicial to the law of the land.According to the ED, the money was moved through a complex network of cash couriers and intermediaries who allegedly collected funds from the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi and delivered them to separatist leaders, including Malik, for subversive activities.The agency has alleged that Malik received foreign funds worth more than Rs 3 crore and laundered the proceeds of crime. It has also accused Shah and Rashid of receiving funds through intermediaries and maintaining links with separatist organisations.The allegations are yet to be established through trial.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: An Australian builder spent years turning a home for his son into a medieval castle with a moat, a dungeon-style games room and water-spouting gargoyles
articles.summary: A family business needed a headquarters, and Australian builder Ray Hollingsworth had an unconventional solution: build a castle.
articles.body: A family business needed a headquarters, and Australian builder Ray Hollingsworth had an unconventional solution: build a castle. The result is a three-storey, castle-style home in Warrnambool, Victoria, featuring a moat, a keep, a dungeon-themed games room and gargoyles that release water when it rains. Hollingsworth, who has worked as a builder for more than five decades, built the castle for his eldest son, Richard. It serves as a home for Richard and his wife and as a base for the brothers’ tabletop war-gaming business. ABC News reported on the project in December 2025, noting the family’s shared interest in medieval stories and fantasy.Why an Australian builder turned a family business headquarters into a medieval castle for his son The idea grew out of a practical need. Richard and his brothers run a tabletop war-gaming business, and Hollingsworth thought they needed an appropriate headquarters. He proposed building a castle. The family had long been interested in knights, dragons and medieval fantasy. Richard’s wedding in 2025 also had a medieval theme. Hollingsworth built the property for Richard, his eldest son. The family’s connection to the building extends beyond its construction: the brothers use the basement for their business, while Richard and his wife have made the castle their home. Richard told ABC that the property was a dream come true, both as a place to live and as a base for their work.Reclaimed church doors, cemetery fencing and an English Axminster carpet add character to the castle The project took shape over several years, with the design evolving as construction progressed. Some of its features came from reclaimed materials rather than purpose-made fittings. The entrance incorporates doors sourced from an old church in a nearby town. Wrought-iron fencing recovered from a cemetery was also put to use, while the Axminster carpet had to be brought over from England after a wait of several months. articles.title: Philippines investigating allegations against Meghan's father
articles.summary: Authorities in the Philippines said they are investigating allegations that Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan Markle, wife of Britain's Prince Harry, ha...
articles.body:
Authorities in the Philippines said they are investigating allegations that Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan Markle, wife of Britain's Prince Harry, had a hoard of child sex abuse images.

According to The Sun, Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged that he found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

He reportedly told police in the country that he discovered the child abuse pictures and videos mixed up with innocent family mementos.

The newspaper said he also contacted FBI investigators in the US in July.

Nicholas Ty, undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, told ITV News: "Our Anti-Trafficking and Online Sexual Abuse and Exploitation of Children taskforce in Cebu is currently investigating the matter."

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Thomas Sr denied possessing child sex images, calling the accusations "sick lies."

On Friday, Meghan said she was made aware of "disturbing allegations" about her father in 2018.

She said she was shown a letter sent to Scotland Yard eight years ago making "troubling" allegations against Thomas Markle Sr and she was assured that these were being investigated.

It is understood the Metropolitan Police has not previously, nor is the force currently, investigating Mr Markle.

The force said it is making internal inquiries regarding officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command being involved in the passing on of a letter.

The FBI said in a statement: "The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities.

"We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."

It is unclear what the nature of the allegations in 2018 were and whether they are linked to the accusations raised by his son now in 2026.

It is understood the letter sent to the Metropolitan Police was shared with Meghan in the summer of 2018, after her wedding to Harry.

Meghan became estranged from her former TV lighting director father in the run-up to her 2018 royal wedding after he was caught staging paparazzi photographs.

Mr Markle did not attend the wedding, leaving the King to accompany Meghan down the aisle and meaning the only member of her family present was her mother, Doria Ragland.

Meghan was the only child of Mr Markle's marriage to Ms Ragland, though he has two children – Samantha and Thomas Jr – from an earlier marriage.

In 2021, Meghan won a High Court privacy and copyright claim against Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL) over articles that reproduced parts of a "personal and private" handwritten letter she wrote to Mr Markle in a bid to get him to stop talking to the press.

She penned the emotional five-page letter to him in August 2018 after taking advice from two unnamed senior royals.

In 2025, Mr Markle moved to the Philippines for a new life after suffering a series of strokes.

Then, in December of that year, he had his leg amputated during life-saving surgery.

Meghan "reached out" to him in the aftermath of the operation, a spokesperson for the duchess revealed, and Meghan was also said to have tried to do so previously.

He is reportedly now living in a rehab centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again.

Buckingham Palace and the Philippine Department of Justice have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: In 1984, George Michael released Last Christmas with Wham!; 40 years later, royalties helped his fund make over 20 grants supporting young people facing hardship, homelessness and mental health struggles
articles.summary: A Christmas song about heartbreak has found a lasting way to help people facing difficult times. Four decades after Wham!
articles.body: A Christmas song about heartbreak has found a lasting way to help people facing difficult times. Four decades after Wham! released Last Christmas, royalties accumulated from sales of the festive hit helped the George Michael Fund make more than 20 grants to organisations supporting children and young people across the UK. The funding, announced to mark the song’s 40th anniversary in 2024, helped provide Christmas gifts to disadvantaged children, counselling for young people struggling with their mental health, and support for LGBTQ+ youth facing homelessness or family estrangement, according to the fund’s official website.The initiative reflects the late singer’s long-standing commitment to charitable giving, which he often did without publicity during his lifetime. His family and executors continued that work after his death in 2016, eventually establishing the George Michael Fund in 2024 to support causes that mattered to him.From a 1984 hit to a charitable legacyWham!, the British pop duo comprising George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley, released Last Christmas on December 3, 1984. Written and produced by Michael, the song became one of the defining festive releases of the decade. It was issued as a double A-side with Everything She Wants and reached No. 2 on the UK singles chart that Christmas, held off the top position by Band Aid’s famine-relief single Do They Know It’s Christmas?, which also featured Michael on vocals.The song’s charitable connection dates back to its release. Michael publicly committed his royalties from Last Christmas to famine relief in Ethiopia, following his involvement with Band Aid. In a 2024 interview with Big Issue, Ridgeley recalled the decision to donate the royalties, explaining that the duo wanted the song to contribute to the relief effort.Over the decades, Last Christmas developed a life of its own, returning to the charts each festive season and reaching No. 1 in the UK for the first time in January 2021. It subsequently became the UK’s official Christmas No. 1 in 2023. Sony Music described it as one of the country’s best-selling singles of all time in its 40th-anniversary announcement in October 2024. The song’s enduring commercial success has helped keep its charitable potential alive.Where the royalties wentThe George Michael Fund’s anniversary initiative directed money to more than 20 organisations working with children and young people throughout the UK. The grants covered several areas of need rather than one single cause.One priority was helping disadvantaged children receive Christmas gifts. The fund said its support contributed to the UK’s biggest gift-giving effort, which aims to ensure that no child wakes up to nothing on Christmas morning.Other grants helped young people experiencing mental health difficulties access counselling. Funding also went to organisations supporting LGBTQ+ young people dealing with family estrangement or homelessness.These issues can overlap. Young people who lose family support or experience rejection may face unstable housing and emotional distress, making access to counselling and specialist services particularly important.The fund has not presented the initiative simply as a one-off anniversary gesture. Its website says the grant-making effort was repeated the following year, extending the connection between the song’s royalties and support for young people.A recipient organisation, Step2, offered a concrete example of how the funding could be used. In a December 2024 announcement, the organisation said it had received funding from the George Michael Fund made possible by royalties from Last Christmas. The grant allowed it to offer additional community counselling sessions at the Mayfield Centre.The announcement illustrates how the song’s commercial earnings could translate into more opportunities for people seeking help, although the published information does not specify the total number of counselling sessions funded across all recipients.A tradition of giving without fanfareMichael’s charitable work extended well beyond the song. According to the George Michael Fund, he established the Mill Charitable Trust in 2009. The trust’s understated name reflected his preference for giving quietly, often without public recognition.After his death on Christmas Day in 2016, his family and executors continued supporting charitable causes. The George Michael Fund was established in 2024 and is managed by The Talent Fund on behalf of the Mill Charitable Trust. Its purpose is to provide grants to organisations and causes that were close to the singer’s heart.The fund says helping young people was an issue Michael cared deeply about throughout his career. Its work aims to preserve that commitment by directing money towards practical support for people facing difficult circumstances.The anniversary grants also demonstrate how music royalties can continue to generate social benefits long after a song is first released. While the recording remains a staple of seasonal playlists, its accumulated earnings can help organisations deliver services that extend beyond the festive period.Four decades on, the song keeps givingThe 40th anniversary of Last Christmas was marked in 2024 with a special release celebrating the original recording and additional material. Sony Music also highlighted the song’s extraordinary longevity, including its repeated returns to the charts and its global popularity.Yet its legacy is not limited to sales, streams or chart positions. The George Michael Fund’s grants have connected the song to work addressing poverty, mental health difficulties, homelessness and family rejection among young people.The fund says it is proud to continue supporting causes that mattered to Michael. For the organisations receiving assistance, the significance lies in the services they can provide and the people they can reach.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1996, a New York couple bought their home believing a tree line marked the boundary; 30 years later, an appeals court revived a privacy claim over cameras filming their backyard and daughter
articles.summary: A New York couple who bought their home in 1996 believing that a line of trees marked the boundary with their neighbour's property have spent years
articles.body: A New York couple who bought their home in 1996 believing that a line of trees marked the boundary with their neighbour's property have spent years fighting over the same stretch of land. What began as a disagreement over where one property ended and the other began eventually involved allegations of trespass and surveillance cameras recording their backyard.Nearly 30 years after the purchase, a New York appeals court has revived the couple's privacy claim after they alleged that their neighbours' cameras captured thousands of images and videos, including footage of their swimming pool and young daughter.According to details of the case available on Justia, the ruling, delivered on Thursday, concerns Timothy J. Riley and his co-plaintiff, who own a home in the Town of Malta, Saratoga County, and their neighbours, John C Daly and his co-defendant. Both properties are part of a four-plot residential development, with the Rileys living on the northern side and the Dalys to the south.The Rileys purchased their property from the developer in December 1996. At the time, they understood that the trees between the two plots marked the boundary. The original neighbour appeared to share that understanding. He watched them maintain the wooded area on their side and later helped them build a garage about 15 feet from the trees.Things began to change in 2004 when the neighbour sold his property to the Dalys. Two years later, the new owners built a chain-link fence between the tree line and the Rileys' garage. The Rileys believed the fence stood on their land. In 2011, they installed their own fence about two feet away. Over time, the disagreement grew into a dispute involving approximately 230 feet of the boundary.Disagreement over trees led to surveillance camerasBy 2018, the dispute had reached the courts. Both households accused each other of wrongdoing in the contested area. The Rileys wanted the boundary they had recognised for years to be legally accepted, while the Dalys maintained that the land belonged to them.But the disagreement was no longer limited to fences and property lines. The Dalys had also installed surveillance cameras, which became a major part of the Rileys' lawsuit.The Dalys told the court that they had installed the cameras to monitor their property following alleged incidents of trespass, theft and harassment. They maintained that the purpose was to prevent further problems, not to harass their neighbours.The Rileys, however, raised concerns about what the cameras were recording. They submitted photographs showing their backyard and swimming pool, including an image of their daughter, who was a minor.They also claimed that information obtained from one of the cameras and during the legal proceedings showed that thousands of photographs or videos had been captured. According to them, the recordings extended beyond the disputed strip of land into other parts of their backyard.Why court allowed privacy claim to continueNew York has a law that protects homeowners against certain types of unwanted surveillance by neighbours. It allows people to seek damages if cameras are installed on adjoining property to record activities in their backyard without written permission and with the intention of harassing, alarming or threatening them.The lower court had earlier dismissed their privacy claim. However, the appeals court disagreed, finding that the photographs and allegations about the recordings raised questions that needed further examination and reinstated the Rileys' invasion of privacy claim.What happened to the original property dispute?While the cameras became an important issue, the question that started the disagreement remained unresolved: Where exactly was the boundary between the two homes?The Rileys argued that the tree line should be recognised because it had been treated as the boundary for years. Under New York law, a boundary accepted by neighbouring owners for more than 10 years can, in certain circumstances, become legally recognised.However, the court found that the Rileys had not provided enough evidence to establish that both households had accepted the trees as the boundary for the required period. The Dalys' decision to build a fence on the Rileys' claimed side of the trees also raised doubts about such an agreement.The Dalys, meanwhile, relied on land surveys to support their ownership claim. But the Rileys pointed out differences between the surveys, arguing that these could shift the boundary by approximately 10 feet.They also alleged that wooden survey stakes and the original natural boundary had been removed before a surveyor inspected the property in 2018.The appeals court found that these differences could not be ignored. It thus overturned the lower court's decision to settle the boundary according to the Dalys' survey.Another disagreement involved allegations that the Rileys had cut or removed trees from the disputed land. The judges found that this issue also required further examination because ownership of the area had not been conclusively established.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Meet Ashaatti Ammumma: Kerala grandmother wins hearts by teaching kids to write in sand
articles.summary: Who ever said you need a slick classroom, a spotless whiteboard, or piles of brand-new workbooks just to teach little kids how to write?
articles.body: Who ever said you need a slick classroom, a spotless whiteboard, or piles of brand-new workbooks just to teach little kids how to write? An elderly grandmother down in Kerala is winning over people all across the internet, showing everyone that real learning doesn't need much - just a dedicated teacher, a pile of sand, and a whole lot of patience.The woman, known locally as Ashaatti Ammumma, starred in a sweet clip shared on Instagram by the account Mom of Safaachiii. In the video, she turns a plain patch of dirt outside into her own little open-air classroom, gathering a bunch of excited kids for their daily writing practice.Turning plain dirt into a blackboardHer entire setup is as low-tech as it gets. Sitting right on the ground with a small container of sand nearby, Ashaatti Ammumma sweeps a light, smooth layer across the earth, leveling it out with a tiny stick.As soon as her makeshift slate is ready, she starts drawing alphabet letters straight into the grit, walking the children through how to form fluid cursive loops. The kids sit cross-legged right across from her, completely locked into the lesson. Forget notebooks, pens, or crayons - they simply reach out and trace every letter directly in the soft sand using their own fingers.You won't spot any pricey school gear, plastic toys, or digital tablets here. It's just a patient teacher and a handful of neighborhood kids picking up foundational skills at their own relaxed pace.Why the internet can't stop sharing her lessonThe heartwarming clip picked up thousands of sweet comments almost overnight, with people loving the nostalgic, back-to-basics feel of early childhood learning.Aside from everyone gushing over how adorable Ashaatti Ammumma is, plenty of viewers highlighted a surprisingly clever practical side: it's a totally eco-friendly, zero-waste setup. If a child messes up a letter or runs out of space, there's no erasing or tearing pages out. They just wipe their hand across the sand, brush it flat, and boom - a fresh canvas in two seconds flat.Other comments pointed out how awesome tactile play is for early development. Feeling that rough, gritty sand under their small fingertips as they form curves actually helps build muscle memory, making it way easier for young brains to remember letter shapes compared to tapping away on a cold iPad screen or staring at a printed book.Proof that real teaching happens anywhereObviously, no one is arguing that a patch of dirt should replace modern schools, textbooks, or actual paper. But Ashaatti Ammumma’s adorable outdoor sessions are a beautiful reality check: good teaching doesn't have to be fancy, expensive, or high-tech to actually work.When you strip everything away, little kids don't need shiny gadgets or overpriced learning kits to stay curious and engaged. Sometimes, all it takes to ignite that spark is a wooden stick, a handful of sand, and a loving grandmother who takes the time to guide them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. November 1 is a day that holds deep emotional significance for the Sikh community, as they remember the 1984 massacre with profound sorrow," Prasad said."So, by creating a storm at Ramlila Maidan on November 1, what kind of salt does Rahul Gandhi want to rub into their wounds?" he asked.The BJP leader also said that many members of the opposition alliance were not satisfied with the decision to hold the rally on November 1."We have heard that many members of their alliance were also not satisfied with this decision. However, since many allies did not attend, the meeting was postponed," he said."We have also learnt that several allies were unhappy with the November 1 date and had suggested that the rally be postponed to a later date. articles.summary: Daniel Craig has taken on a new role away from Hollywood by becoming the co-owner of a historic London pub alongside Soho House founder Nick Jones and two
articles.body: Daniel Craig has taken on a new role away from Hollywood by becoming the co-owner of a historic London pub alongside Soho House founder Nick Jones and two other hospitality figures. The Horseshoe in Clerkenwell has a history stretching back to at least 1748 and is known for its traditional atmosphere and darts-playing regulars. The new owners plan to refurbish the pub over the next year while preserving its character and keeping it welcoming to ordinary customers. However, the venue has another talking point beyond its celebrity owners. Its former landlady says a ghost named Gilbert haunts the cellar. Craig has responded to the story with humour, joking that the spirit might have to be offered a pint when the pub reopens.Daniel Craig and Nick Jones take over historic London pubThe former James Bond actor has joined forces with Nick Jones, founder of the members' club group Soho House, to take over The Horseshoe in Clerkenwell. The partnership also includes Charlie Carroll, founder of the Flat Iron steakhouse chain and a co-founder of The Devonshire pub in Soho, and Justin O'Shea, creative director of the lager brand Bad Belze, which he launched with Craig.The pub had been run by Richard and Pauline Tucker for 36 years before the couple retired. The new owners plan to give the venue a major refurbishment while retaining its identity as a traditional neighbourhood pub.Craig has said he does not want to turn the Horseshoe into an exclusive gastropub aimed only at customers willing to spend heavily. Instead, the aim is to preserve the welcoming atmosphere that has made traditional pubs important gathering places for local communities.The Horseshoe has a history stretching back to the 18th centuryLocated on Clerkenwell Close in central London, The Horseshoe has existed on the site since at least 1748, according to the Campaign for Real Ale. Over the years, it became known as a traditional local pub with a beer garden and an upstairs room used for darts.The venue attracted regular customers who came to play darts, meet friends and spend time in a familiar setting. Its long-running connection with the local community was a defining part of its identity under the Tuckers.The new owners intend to preserve the pub's traditional character while improving its facilities. Their plans reflect an effort to give the historic venue a new lease of life without losing the qualities that made it popular with regulars.The cellar ghost named GilbertThe pub's most unusual story concerns a ghost known as Gilbert. Pauline Tucker told The Times that the spirit was believed to be a former hangman who haunted the cellar.“You don’t see him. You feel him,” Tucker said when describing the alleged presence.According to reports, the new owners had not been told about the ghost before the sale. The story came to light as the pub prepared to close for its renovation.Craig appeared unfazed by the tale. Speaking to The Times, he joked that the owners might need to leave a drink for the spirit, saying: “I don’t know what he drinks but we might have to leave a pint down there: ‘Here you are Gilbert’.”The account remains a local legend rather than a verified supernatural occurrence. Nevertheless, it has added an unusual twist to the pub's change of ownership.What the year-long refurbishment will changeThe Horseshoe closed in October 2026 ahead of a renovation expected to take around a year. The plans include converting the upstairs area, which has been used for darts, into a dining room. The owners also intend to add a terrace and a sizeable beer garden.The ground floor is expected to retain its role as a traditional pub serving drinks and simple food. Carroll will oversee the food offering, drawing on his experience with Flat Iron and The Devonshire.Bad Belze, the lager brand launched by Craig and O'Shea, is also expected to feature at the venue. The group hopes to improve the pub while keeping it accessible to a broad range of customers.A confirmed reopening date has not been announced, although published reports have indicated that the pub could reopen in late 2027.Daniel Craig's family connection to pubsCraig's new venture has a personal connection to his upbringing. His parents ran the Ring O'Bells pub in Frodsham, Cheshire, while his grandparents owned another pub in Chester.As a child, Craig spent time around the pubs and spoke to the local customers who visited them. He has recalled the celebrations and late-night gatherings that were part of family life in the trade.He has also spoken about the role pubs play in their communities. For Craig, they are places where people can meet, catch up and talk about their problems as much as places to eat and drink.His experience has shaped his approach to The Horseshoe. Rather than creating a venue that caters only to celebrities or wealthy customers, he wants it to remain a place where ordinary people feel comfortable.A new chapter for The HorseshoeThe takeover brings a historic Clerkenwell pub into the hands of a group with experience in restaurants, hospitality and drinks. Its renovation will give the owners a chance to improve the building while preserving its traditional identity.The story of Gilbert the alleged cellar ghost may draw curiosity, but the larger challenge will be maintaining the atmosphere that kept the pub going for generations. The new owners will need to balance modern facilities with the character of a long-established local venue.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Seven Italian students built a paper aircraft with a 20-metre wingspan and successfully flew it inside a hangar
articles.summary: A paper aircraft measuring more than 20 metres across its wings has set a Guinness World Records title after successfully flying inside an aeroplane
articles.body: A paper aircraft measuring more than 20 metres across its wings has set a Guinness World Records title after successfully flying inside an aeroplane hangar in Bologna, Italy. Created by students from the University of Pisa, the giant aircraft, named Icarus, was made entirely from paper and glue. Its successful flight on 25 June 2026 marked the end of months of planning, testing and construction. According to the University of Pisa, the aircraft travelled 59 metres, surpassing a record that had remained unbroken since 2013.How did seven Italian students build the record-breaking paper aircraftAccording to Guinness World Records, the project began with a simple idea shared by engineering students during their university lectures. The group discovered the existing record while studying for exams and decided to attempt something that had previously seemed difficult to achieve on such a scale.The previous record belonged to the Braunschweig Institute of Technology in Germany, whose paper aircraft had a wingspan of 18.21 metres. That achievement had stood since 2013, giving the Italian students a clear target to beat.The University of Pisa reported that the project was developed by its engineering students with support from science communicator and content creator Jakidale. What started as an informal idea developed into a substantial engineering challenge involving design, calculations, testing and construction.The team eventually expanded its efforts beyond the original seven students, bringing in 16 additional helpers to contribute to the technical and production work. The collaboration helped turn the idea into an aircraft large enough to challenge the existing world record.Icarus is different from an ordinary paper planeThe finished aircraft measured 20.04 metres from one wingtip to the other and approximately seven metres in length. Guinness World Records lists its weight at around 28.5 kilograms, making it a substantial structure despite being constructed using only paper and glue.The scale of Icarus presented a different challenge from making a conventional paper plane. A small model can be folded and thrown by hand, but a structure measuring several metres requires careful planning to maintain its shape and travel through the air successfully.According to Guinness World Records, the students used computer simulations to predict how their design might perform before committing to the final construction. These simulations helped them explore the aircraft's proportions and consider how the finished structure could be made to fly.The University of Pisa confirmed that the final aircraft was built by hand using paper and glue. Keeping to these materials was central to the challenge, as the team needed to produce a record-breaking aircraft without relying on a conventional frame or other structural materials.How did the team develop the aircraft before its record attemptThe journey towards Icarus involved several stages rather than one successful design from the beginning. Guinness World Records reported that the team built two earlier prototypes before arriving at the final version.The first large model was named Prometheus, after the figure from Greek mythology associated with bringing fire and technology to humanity. It helped the students explore the structural elements needed for a much larger paper aircraft.Their next attempt, Daedalus, measured 8 metres in length and was also constructed from paper and glue. Although it did not perform perfectly, it gave the group practical experience with the materials and highlighted areas that needed improvement.The team then developed a smaller model measuring four metres. This version successfully glided through the air, offering an important demonstration that their approach could work.These experiments allowed the students to learn from earlier designs before committing to the final aircraft. The final aircraft was named Icarus, after the mythological son of Daedalus who attempted to fly. The name reflected the project's central ambition, although the students approached the challenge through careful preparation rather than relying on a single attempt.What happened when the giant paper aircraft finally flewThe record attempt took place on 25 June 2026 at the We Make Future event at BolognaFiere in Bologna. The event, associated with the European Institute of Innovation and Technology's business and entrepreneurship activities, provided a public setting for the aircraft's first major flight.According to Guinness World Records, the team positioned Icarus on scaffolding before preparing to launch it across the hangar. One of the students carried the aircraft into position and prepared to throw it towards the opposite side of the indoor space.The launch required a coordinated effort because of the aircraft's size. Once it was ready, the student ran along the scaffolding and released the plane.The aircraft briefly caught the air before gliding forwards and gradually descending towards the concrete floor. Its movement resembled that of an ordinary paper plane, although its enormous dimensions made the flight a unique sight for the watching crowd.The University of Pisa confirmed that Icarus travelled 59 metres during the successful attempt. Guinness World Records lists the achievement under the title of largest paper aircraft, with the record officially established in Bologna on 25 June.Importance of the achievement for the University of PisaThe successful flight brought an end to a 13-year wait for a new holder of the largest paper aircraft record. According to the University of Pisa, the achievement returned the title to Italy after the previous record had remained with the German institution since 2013.Guinness World Records adjudicator Lorenzo Veltri presented the team with its record certificate after the aircraft's successful launch. He praised the combination of engineering knowledge, teamwork and technological creativity that had made the achievement possible.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2024, a Maine grandfather's home was listed for $225,000 but sold to his stepgrandson for $105,000; after his death, his granddaughter claimed relatives diverted her inheritance, and the state's highest court revived her lawsuit
articles.summary: Family, property and financial power can combine to complicate inheritance disputes.
articles.body: Family, property and financial power can combine to complicate inheritance disputes. A Maine case involving a grandfather’s home, a deeply discounted sale and a contested estate is headed back to court after the state’s highest court ruled a granddaughter had shown enough to pursue her claims. Scroll down to read the details of this property dispute.A will that left everything to his granddaughterAccording to Justia US Law, the October 2026 case involves grandfather Steven of Maine, who named his granddaughter, Ms Sabin, in his will. Steven had three children, one of whom was Sabin's father, who had predeceased him. According to the terms of the will, Sabin was to have the share which would otherwise have gone to her father.In 2022, as he and his wife began to suffer cognitive decline, Steven gave his stepson broad financial power of attorney. It gave the stepson wide-ranging powers over Steven's property, including the power to convey assets and make gifts.However, the power of attorney did not relieve liability for conduct involving dishonesty, an improper motive or reckless disregard of its purposes.Selling a house for $225,000The feud intensified following Steven's wife's death in February 2024, which left Steven the sole owner of the family home.Sabin’s lawsuit says the property was up for sale at $225,000 in March 2024. The stepson had already agreed to sell the property to his son, for a much lower price than its worth, according to the suit. The home changed hands for $105,000 on March 29, with a $5,000 seller credit.Sabin claimed the use of a real estate agent gave the impression of a typical sale considering that the transaction had already been arranged within the family.Proceeds from the sale were deposited into a joint account held by stepchildren and Steven. Stepchildren allegedly received the money instead of it going into the estate when Steven died on June 21, 2024. Sabin also disputed the lack of baseball cards and antique coins and claimed other assets were diverted.Her case was dismissed by lower courtIn March 2025 Sabin sued in Franklin County Superior Court, claiming someone interfered with an inheritance she expected to receive. She asked the court for various remedies, including a constructive trust and punitive damages.The Superior Court dismissed the case later that year, stating that she had not sufficiently established the nature and extent of the inheritance she was to receive. Sabin appealed the ruling. The Maine supreme judicial court disagreed.Supreme Court revives lawsuitOn Oct. 22, 2026, the court ruled that Sabin had adequately alleged an expectancy of inheritance. At this stage of the proceedings her status as Steven’s granddaughter, her status in the will and her allegations regarding the house and other property were sufficient.The defendants also failed to convince the court that they were shielded from liability by Steven’s power of attorney. As a matter of Maine law, an agent cannot escape liability for acts done dishonestly or with an improper purpose.Importantly, the ruling does not mean that Sabin will ultimately win her claim to the inheritance. Rather, it means that her allegations are enough to go forward, and there remains evidence to be reviewed about the value and disposition of Steven’s property.The dismissal has been overturned by the Supreme Judicial Court, which has sent the case back to the lower court for further action. The case has revived a family inheritance fight that began over the sale of a house, and now centers on events surrounding the estate both before and after the death of Steven.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: Why do some women become the strongest defenders of patriarchy
articles.summary: Oxford dictionary defines feminism as 'the belief and aim that women should have the same rights and opportunities as men or the struggle to achieve this
articles.body: “Sir, let me say that I am not a feminist. I consider myself as a human being. As a human being we feel that it is our duty to help women, minorities, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, OBCs, and also the neglected class.”Oxford dictionary defines feminism as 'the belief and aim that women should have the same rights and opportunities as men or the struggle to achieve this aim.'Then why is it that some of us distance ourselves from this term? And why is it that some women uphold the very patriarchy that restricts them?Why do some women keep patriarchy aliveA group called the NCMIndia Council for Men Affairs recently took out a 'Long Live Patriarchy' march that went viral on social media. The group also had women holding the banner. "In the name of equality, these girls don't want to do jhaadu-pocha, clean utensils or raise kids. They just want freedom, money and debauchery," one of the women at the march said. "Equality does not mean freedom to drink, smoke, roam around at night. Women are misusing their independence. Azaadi does not mean shaming men."TOI spoke to Dolly Kumari, who is also a member of the group that actively raises men's issues, and asked her what patriarchy meant to her."Patriarchy cannot be understood simply as a system created by men to oppress women. When a woman speaks about men's issues, some people may find it surprising because they expect her to speak only from a particular gender-based perspective. But I do not believe empathy should have a gender. Supporting men who experience injustice does not mean denying the difficulties women face," she said."My objection is to the idea that everything traditional must be condemned as patriarchal and, therefore, bad. If a man wants to protect and provide for his family, and a woman willingly chooses to trust him in that role, why should society automatically call that oppression or brainwashed women?"Oxford dictionary defines patriarchy as '​a society, system or country that is ruled or controlled by men.' It would appear, then, that women supporting patriarchy would be an anomaly. However, Dolly said that the purpose of their 'Long Live Patriarchy' initiative was to raise awareness of men's rights, which "we have been organising on Gandhi Jayanti for nearly a decade.""Equality should not become a competition between men and women. Women deserve justice, and so do men. We need a society where both can express their pain, seek support, and live with dignity without being judged by gender stereotypes," said Dolly."In the traditional Indian family, men were often expected to provide, protect and take responsibility for their families while women traditionally took on many responsibilities related to the home and children. These roles evolved within the social and economic realities of their time although it resulted in unequal rights and restrictions. Our history is not simply a story of oppression and therefore patriarchy should prevail."Is the 'aurat hi aurat ki dushman' concept real? Does different treatment of a son from daughter and parenting play a role in keeping misogyny alive? Or is this 'aurat hi aurat ki dushman hoti hai' syndrome.Devika Anand, a psychologist at Rise and Mind, believes that the answer lies partly in the way gender roles are normalised within families and communities."I think one way to understand this is that we don't always question the systems we grow up in, particularly when those systems are presented to us as normal, moral, or necessary. When a woman grows up learning that a good woman is one who sacrifices, adjusts, tolerates, or puts others before herself, these expectations can become deeply embedded in her understanding of what it means to be a woman," she said.Over time, these expectations may stop feeling like restrictions and start being seen as values. A woman may even derive a sense of identity or self-worth from having lived up to them, sometimes at considerable personal cost."When younger women choose differently, it can challenge not just her beliefs but also the meaning she has attached to her own sacrifices," Devika explained.This explains why some women who have experienced restrictions themselves may go on to impose similar expectations on younger women. Having spent years adjusting to restrictive norms, they may come to regard them as an inevitable part of life rather than something that can be challenged."There can also be a need to make sense of one's own experiences. If someone has made significant sacrifices because she believed there was no alternative, acknowledging that those sacrifices were unnecessary or unfair can be painful. It may bring up feelings of anger, grief, or regret. Believing that younger women must make similar sacrifices can sometimes help preserve the sense that those sacrifices had a purpose," Devika said.When certain expectations are repeatedly reinforced within families and communities, they can become the default way of relating to others. A woman may reproduce the same expectations she experienced, not necessarily because she wants younger women to suffer, but because she has learned to see those expectations as responsible or appropriate behaviour.Can patriarchy give women a sense of power? "Power doesn't always mean having equal power within a system. Sometimes, it means having more power than someone else within that system," Devika said.In a patriarchal family, a woman may have limited autonomy in relation to men but still hold considerable authority over younger women, daughters-in-law or other women in the household. She may have little influence over the rules themselves but gain status by enforcing them."This can give her a sense of belonging, security, or control in an environment where her own power is otherwise limited," Devika explained.There can also be a psychological incentive to conform. If a woman receives approval, respect or recognition for upholding family traditions, questioning those traditions may threaten not only her beliefs but also her position within the family or community.When tradition becomes a question of freedom Calling kindness, compassion, empathy and nurture 'qualities' that women should have, Dolly said, "I feel that relationships are increasingly being discussed in terms of personal freedom, sometimes without equal emphasis on duties, compromise, commitment, and mutual accountability."Dolly believes that a woman does not have to reject tradition to prove that she is empowered. "I come from a traditional, patriarchal family, yet my father always encouraged me to participate in activities that people might traditionally associate with boys. I played sports, learned to ride a bike, built a career in technology, and today have a beautiful family of my own. Growing up with two brothers also gave me a personal experience of sharing opportunities and responsibilities across gender lines. That experience is one of the reasons I believe that having a traditional father or growing up in a strict household does not automatically mean being oppressed. Tradition and discipline are not inherently oppressive," she said.Devika, too, cautions against labelling every woman who holds a traditional belief as a victim of internalised misogyny, which may include judging women more harshly than men, policing other women's behaviour, or believing that women are inherently less capable or less deserving of autonomy," she said.When women challenge the rules they grew up with A 65-year old influencer from Haryana called Tai Savitri, who recently went viral over her commentary on society and patriarchy, told TOI that even though her experiences have been bitter, it was her educated children that taught her to become a feminist. "I was less educated. My kids got good education so I learnt a few things from them. It was also a feeling that I should do something for the women," she told TOI.She recalled facing criticism in her village, even though her family did not offer much resistance to her views."Yes, I have also heard that aurat hi aurat ki dushman hoti hai but I think it is more because of lack of education that pitied one woman against the other, a system wherein one woman was the slave of another. This created a scenario where women did not want other women to succeed in life," she said.In one of her viral videos, Savitri compared women who restrict other women to dogs that have become accustomed to living on a leash. "You must have seen dog owners taking their pets out. Even if they let go of this leash, by mistake or deliberately, you will notice that the dog itself will hold the leash in his mouth and give it back to his owner. Because the dog has now developed a habit of living like a slave and it has accepted its fate. It is the same with women who try to show other women in poor light. It is the same slave mentality. My only message to women is kutta nahi sher bano (don't be a dog, be a tiger). Whoever tries to put a leash on you or make you a slave, rip them to shreds," she said.Patriarchy gives some women a sense of belonging There is a distinction between having a choice and the freedom to make that choice. Holding a traditional belief is not the same as denying another woman the right to choose differently. The consequences of that belief, and the degree to which it is imposed on others, matter.Women who defend patriarchal expectations are not necessarily motivated by a single cause. Their views may be shaped by the values they grew up with, the sacrifices they have made, the security they derive from their place within a family or community, or a genuine belief that traditional arrangements offer stability.The question, then, is not simply why some women become flagbearers of patriarchy. It is also why a system that can restrict women's choices sometimes offers them identity, belonging or authority in return—and what it would take for women to feel secure enough to question it.Perhaps the more useful question is not whether women are their own enemies, but whether a society that teaches women to measure their worth through sacrifice, obedience and conformity gives them enough room to imagine a different way of living.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘No hesitation in detaining youth’: Congress targets government over US national VanDyke’s release in Myanmar arms case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress on Saturday questioned the decision to allow US national Matthew VanDyke, an accused in the Myanmar arms training case, to return to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Saturday questioned the decision to allow US national Matthew VanDyke, an accused in the Myanmar arms training case, to return to his home country, asking why a foreign national accused of terrorism was being granted such liberty while young activists protesting against alleged “vote chori” were being detained.Congress general secretary in charge of communications Jairam Ramesh raised the issue in a post on X, referring to VanDyke's release and the extension of permission for him and six Ukrainian nationals to remain outside India until February 24 next year.“US national Matthew VanDyke, arrested for conspiring to carry out terrorist activities against India, was released yesterday and allowed to return home for 4 months. Why has such liberty been extended to a foreign national accused of terrorism?” Ramesh asked.He also criticised the government's handling of protests against alleged electoral irregularities.“This even as the government has shown no hesitation in detaining and arresting youth activists and peaceful protesters during the anti-vote chori protests this past month,” he said.Ramesh further pointed to the issue being raised during US secretary of state Marco Rubio's visit to India in May, noting that the American official had visited again this week.Congress raises questions over US interventionRamesh had previously accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of being a “compromised PM” following VanDyke's release in September.The Congress leader had claimed that Rubio raised the matter during his May visit to India and that US ambassador to India Sergio Gor also took it up with foreign secretary Vikram Misri.On September 8, Ramesh claimed that charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) had been dropped against VanDyke. He alleged that this contrasted with what he described as the widespread misuse of the law against Indian citizens and delays in such cases.After VanDyke was released on September 24, Ramesh alleged that the prime minister had “failed” to protect India's elections, institutions and national security.Court allows seven accused to remain abroad till February 24A Delhi court on Friday extended until February 24, 2027, the permission granted to VanDyke and six Ukrainian nationals to remain outside India while the National Investigation Agency (NIA) continues its probe into the Myanmar arms training case.Special Judge Prashant Sharma passed the order after hearing applications filed by the seven accused. The proceedings were held in-camera.The NIA sought additional time to investigate several aspects of the case, with its counsel Rahul Tyagi making submissions to that effect. The agency told the court that further investigation was needed to verify alleged offences under the UAPA in connection with the import and recovery of large quantities of drones and accessories through India.VanDyke appeared in person before the court on Friday and was permitted to return to the US.The other six accused attended the hearing through video conferencing, citing health issues.The seven foreign nationals had earlier been permitted to stay in their home countries until October 23 after seeking six weeks to meet their families.NIA alleges training of armed groups in MyanmarThe NIA has alleged that VanDyke and the six Ukrainian nationals entered India on tourist visas, travelled to the northeastern region without the required permits and crossed from Mizoram into Myanmar, where they allegedly trained ethnic armed organisations.The accused were arrested on March 13 over allegations of training insurgent-linked groups in Myanmar.The agency had initially invoked provisions of the UAPA, including those relating to conspiracy.However, its chargesheet did not include the UAPA provisions and instead invoked Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act. These provisions cover offences that can be compounded before the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO).The NIA had previously indicated that its investigation into the alleged terror-related aspects was continuing and that further allegations could be included in a supplementary chargesheet.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US on alert as Iran's plan to target Americans abroad in 'advanced stages': Report
articles.summary: The United States is reducing staffing at four embassies in the Middle East reportedly after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to
articles.body: The United States is reducing staffing at four embassies in the Middle East reportedly after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel overseas, adding to security concerns as the Trump administration weighs its next move in the conflict with Tehran.The broader security concerns came into focus after director of national intelligence Jay Clayton warned Secretary of State Marco Rubio that alleged Iranian plots against American citizens had reached an advanced stage. “The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” Clayton wrote in an unclassified memo dated October 23, as reported by CBS News.Clayton said Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel”. The memo did not specify the intended targets or countries involved, or establish whether any attacks were imminent. CIA director John Ratcliffe was copied on the communication.The diplomatic drawdowns affect US missions in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, which will continue operating under restrictions. The move follows an earlier order for non-essential personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.The intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive information gathered through various channels so that it can be shared more widely with State Department personnel. The memo was first reported by Axios and subsequently obtained by CBS News and The Associated Press.Iran threat and Houthi attacks drive security measuresWashington has cited the threat from the Houthis, who have intensified missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, as a reason for tightening security at diplomatic facilities. US officials have also linked the latest staffing adjustments to alleged Iranian plots against American officials.“When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” a US official told CBS News.“The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting UD officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region,” the official said.Thus, while non-essential personnel and their families have been ordered to leave Saudi Arabia, the four other embassies remain open under restricted operations, with staff not required to depart.The security alert comes against the backdrop of a wider regional conflict that has put American personnel, energy infrastructure and commercial shipping at risk. The Houthis have allegedly targeted Saudi oil facilities and airports, while Iran has continued to claim responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.Iran's Revolutionary Guard has also threatened US military bases in the region over American assistance to commercial shipping through the strategic waterway, according to reports carried by The Associated Press.Trump keeps option of renewed strikes 'open'The intelligence warning comes as diplomatic efforts to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal negotiations face uncertainty. Although the two countries have not exchanged direct strikes in recent weeks, Trump has not ruled out resuming military action.At a rally in Florida on Friday, Trump suggested the United States could launch another operation if Iran failed to reach an agreement. “We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree,” he said, referring to the US military campaign launched in February.US officials have denied that the latest embassy staffing reductions are connected to preparations for possible new American and Israeli strikes on Iran, according to AP. The moves have instead been attributed to the deteriorating security environment and threats against US personnel.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Power of multi-stakeholder model of engagement for remote and challenging terrains
articles.summary: Across India, numerous social impact initiatives are being undertaken to support and accelerate the nation's development journey.
articles.body: Across India, numerous social impact initiatives are being undertaken to support and accelerate the nation's development journey. However, for any project to be truly effective and sustainable, it is essential to collaborate with the right stakeholders who can contribute meaningfully to the cause.Particular attention must be given to India's remote and far-flung regions, especially the border areas in the northern and northeastern parts of the country. These locations often face unique challenges due to their difficult terrain, limited accessibility, and fewer opportunities compared to urban centers and developed regions. Many individuals and young people living in these areas continue to face hardships and limited access to resources, education, skilling, and livelihood opportunities.When we think about creating social impact at a national level, it is crucial to consider how we can strengthen the communities residing in these regions. Due to geographical barriers and logistical challenges, reaching these communities is often difficult. As a result, many such areas remain relatively underserved and require greater focus and attention.As the pace of development across India continues to accelerate, it becomes increasingly important to ensure that these regions progress alongside the rest of the country. Inclusive development can only be achieved when every community, regardless of location, has access to opportunities for growth and empowerment.To successfully implement social impact initiatives in such remote and challenging terrains, identifying and engaging the right stakeholders is critical. These stakeholders should be individuals and organizations that are trusted by the local communities, understand the local context, and ideally belong to the region itself. Their participation helps build trust, and acceptance among community members.At the same time, it is important to recognize that for many communities in these remote locations, external organizations are often viewed as outsiders. Therefore, any effort to work with them must be driven by genuine intent and a selfless commitment to strengthening the community rather than pursuing personal gain, recognition, power, or financial interests.Creating an effective multi-stakeholder model of engagement is essential because each stakeholder brings unique strengths, experiences, and expertise to the table. Such collaboration becomes even more impactful when all partners share a common purpose of community development and collective progress.If we can establish and nurture selfless, community-centered models of engagement in India's remote and border regions, we can significantly strengthen both local communities and the nation as a whole. Meaningful progress in these areas will contribute not only to regional development but also to a stronger, more inclusive India.As individuals, while we continue to build our careers, develop our skills, and support our families, we must also consciously contribute to the well-being of our communities and our nation. By sharing our knowledge, skills, and resources, we can help create opportunities for others to grow and thrive.If collective action through multi-stakeholder partnerships can be mobilized across difficult terrains and remote regions throughout India, we can help ensure that these communities keep pace with the rapid progress taking place in our cities and across the world.Ultimately, we are all interconnected. As we move forward in life, we must consciously strive to uplift and strengthen the people around us, ensuring that development reaches every corner of our country and benefits every community.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Forced to drop out of school for a year when her father could not pay the fees, Mavis Tak failed the UPSC exam twice before clearing it and is now a 2022-batch IPS officer serving as ASP in Uttar Pradesh’s Sonbhadra
articles.summary: When Mavis Tak was a school student, financial difficulties forced her and her elder sister to stay away from school for a year because their father could
articles.body: When Mavis Tak was a school student, financial difficulties forced her and her elder sister to stay away from school for a year because their father could not afford their tuition fees. Years later, after two unsuccessful attempts at the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Civil Services Examination, she cleared it in her third attempt and joined the Indian Police Service (IPS). Today, Tak is a 2022-batch IPS officer of the Uttar Pradesh cadre and serves as Additional Superintendent of Police (ASP) in Sonbhadra district. She is the first woman IPS officer to hold the ASP post there. According to the official website of UP police, her appointment took effect on September 19, 2026.Her journey from a family that struggled to pay school fees to a career in the police service also reflects her father Abdul Karim Tak’s determination to educate his three daughters, despite criticism from relatives and members of society.Her father faced questions about educating his daughtersAccording to the official website of UP police, Mavis was born on September 24, 1996, in Falna, in Rajasthan’s Pali district. As reported by NDTV, her father moved the family to Mumbai in 2003 in search of better economic opportunities. He worked in different roles, including typing and translation assignments, to support the family.The financial pressure affected the children’s education. Mavis and her elder sister had to leave school for a year when their father could not pay their tuition fees. Their father continued working to support the family and ensure that his daughters could resume their studies. The family also faced social criticism over spending money on girls’ education. In an interview with NDTV, Mavis recalled that people questioned her father’s decision to educate his daughters, asking, “What will you make them by educating them so much? a collector or an SP?”Her father did not allow such remarks to determine their future. He encouraged all three daughters to study and pursue careers. According to an earlier report by TOI, Abdul Karim had himself been unable to clear the civil services examination. He subsequently devoted himself to helping his daughters pursue the ambition he had not achieved. Mavis acknowledged the importance of her parents’ support in a 2022 interview with TOI. “My father is my main support and both my parents are pillars who stood behind me and helped me become what I am today,” she said.From a school dropout to a postgraduate degreeTak completed her early schooling in Rajasthan before moving to Mumbai with her family. She later studied at New Cambridge School and Royal College of Arts, Science and Commerce in Mumbai, according to NDTV. She graduated in political science and went on to pursue postgraduate studies in Indian Federation and Language Politics. Her education gave her the academic background to begin preparing for the civil services examination. Her father’s dream of seeing his daughters enter public service influenced her decision to pursue the UPSC examination.Two failed UPSC attempts, then AIR 386Tak first appeared for the UPSC Civil Services Examination in 2019. She was unable to clear the preliminary examination in her first two attempts. Instead of abandoning her plans, she continued preparing and worked on the areas where she had struggled. She relied on self-study rather than joining a coaching institute, as per various media reports.Her third attempt brought the result she had been working towards. She secured All India Rank 386 in the UPSC Civil Services Examination 2021, earning selection to the Indian Police Service (IPS). As per a TOI report in August 2022, she was the first woman from Mira-Bhayandar to clear the civil services examination and secure the IPS cadre. Her college in Mira Road invited her to unfurl the national flag at its Independence Day celebrations and felicitated her for the achievement.Her posting in SonbhadraTak is a member of the 2022-batch Uttar Pradesh cadre. Before her transfer to Sonbhadra, she served in Banda district, where she held responsibilities including Circle Officer (City), Cyber and Crime. The Uttar Pradesh government transferred her to Sonbhadra in September 2026. Her appointment marked the first time a woman IPS officer held the ASP post in Sonbhadra, according to NDTV.Tak’s story has received attention not only because she cleared the UPSC examination without coaching, but also because of the circumstances in which she pursued her education.You use AI every day.
